nodes.name: Compare fractions by rewriting over a common denominator
nodes.statement: Compare two fractions by rewriting both over a common denominator with the multiplication principle; the fraction with the greater rewritten numerator is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 5/6 or 7/9? Show your work.
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two denominators (the product of the denominators always works).
Rewrite each fraction over that denominator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
Compare the rewritten numerators; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction, and equal numerators mean the fractions are equal.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two denominators, which uses the idea of multiples of a whole number.
Step 3 compares the rewritten numerators, which is exactly comparing two fractions that share a denominator.
The statement rewrites fractions with the multiplication principle, which guarantees each rewritten fraction equals the original.
Step 2 rewrites each fraction over the common denominator by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number.

nodes.name: Compare fractions by rewriting with a common numerator
nodes.statement: Compare two fractions with nonzero numerators by rewriting both with a common numerator; the fraction with the smaller rewritten denominator is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 2/3 or 3/5? Compare them by making the numerators the same.
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two numerators (the product of the numerators always works).
Rewrite each fraction with that numerator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
Compare the rewritten denominators; the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction, and equal denominators mean the fractions are equal.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two numerators, which uses multiples of whole numbers.
Step 3 compares the rewritten denominators, which is exactly comparing two fractions that share a numerator.
Step 2 rewrites each fraction with the common numerator by multiplying numerator and denominator by one whole number.

nodes.name: Compare fractions using a benchmark fraction
nodes.statement: Compare two fractions by comparing each to a benchmark such as 1/2 or 1; this decides the comparison only when the two fractions fall on opposite sides of the benchmark.
nodes.assess: Use 1/2 to decide which is greater, 3/8 or 4/7.
procedure: Choose a benchmark, 1/2 or 1.
Compare each fraction to the benchmark (a/b is greater than 1/2 exactly when 2 x a is greater than b, and greater than 1 exactly when a is greater than b).
If one fraction is above the benchmark and the other below, the one above is greater; otherwise this method does not decide, and another method is needed.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test for the benchmark 1/2 compares the whole numbers 2 x a and b.
The test that a/b exceeds 1/2 exactly when 2 x a exceeds b compares a/b with 1/2 over the common denominator 2 x b.
Choosing 1/2 or 1 as a benchmark makes precise the informal size reasoning of placing a fraction above or below a familiar fraction.
Testing whether a/b exceeds 1 compares a/b with b/b, two fractions with the same denominator.
The test against the benchmark 1 writes 1 as b/b so that a/b and b/b can be compared by numerators.

nodes.name: Justify a comparison of fractions with unlike numerators and denominators
nodes.statement: A comparison of two fractions with different numerators and different denominators is justified by a model of the same whole in which both fractions are shown with parts of a common size, so the numbers of parts can be compared.
nodes.assess: Use a fraction model to show why 2/3 > 3/5.

proposed_edges.rationale: The unlike-denominator justification extends the general justification of a fraction comparison by a model of the same whole.
Once both fractions are shown in parts of a common size, the numbers of parts are compared as with a shared denominator.
The model must show both fractions as parts of one and the same whole or the comparison has no meaning.
Showing both fractions with parts of a common size means replacing each by an equivalent amount of the same whole.
Building the model with parts of a common size requires subdividing the parts of each fraction to generate equivalent fractions in the model.

nodes.name: A fraction as a sum of unit fractions
nodes.statement: For any whole number a and denominator b, a/b is the sum of a copies of 1/b, including when a is greater than b (for example, 5/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4).

A fraction a/b is built from a parts of size 1/b, which is what the sum of a unit fractions counts.

nodes.name: Adding fractions as joining parts of the same whole
nodes.statement: Adding two fractions means joining their parts into one amount, where both fractions refer to the same whole.
nodes.assess: Using one bar as the whole, draw what 2/5 + 1/5 means and say what the sum counts.

proposed_edges.rationale: Adding fractions as joining extends the meaning of whole-number addition as putting two amounts together.
The statement requires both fractions to refer to the same whole, which is the same-whole condition.
The amounts being joined are fractions understood as numbers of equal parts of a whole.

nodes.name: Subtracting fractions as separating parts of the same whole
nodes.statement: Subtracting one fraction from another means separating the parts of the second from the parts of the first, where both fractions refer to the same whole.
nodes.assess: Using one bar as the whole, draw what 4/6 - 1/6 means and say what the difference counts.

nodes.name: Add fractions with like denominators using a model

procedure: Check that the denominators are the same.
Add the numerators.
Write the sum over the common denominator.

nodes.name: Subtract fractions with like denominators using a model

nodes.name: Decompose a fraction into a sum of same-denominator fractions with a model

nodes.name: A mixed number as a whole number plus a fraction

proposed_edges.rationale: The model must show the decimals read as numbers of tenths and hundredths of one whole.
The model can be a number line on which each decimal is located as a point.
Decimals such as 0.5 must be read as a number of tenths to shade them.
Justifying a decimal comparison with a model of the same whole parallels justifying a fraction comparison.
Judging which decimal covers more of the grid is comparing counts of hundredths.
The grid or number line must show both decimals on the same whole to compare them.
A hundredths grid shows a decimal as a number of the 100 equal parts of one whole.
Showing 0.5 on a hundredths grid needs 5 tenths seen as 50 hundredths.
